The OCR layer is complete; its first line (']Executive 1t'rer') is the misread heading 'Executive Order', not order text. The order directs that the executive offices of the United States be closed, that the national flag be displayed at half-mast on all Federal buildings, forts, military posts, naval stations and vessels of the United States, and that the representatives of the United States in foreign countries pay tribute in like manner, 'on Thursday, April 15, 1915, the fiftieth anniversary of his death' (Abraham Lincoln's). Its second paragraph only requests owners and masters of merchant ships to display the flag at half-mast; a request is not a command. Identity: number, date and subject agree across the scan, the registry record (signing date 1915-04-13) and the census register. First end: by its own terms at the close of 1915-04-15, the only day it governs; a reader who dates cessation to the first day without effect would write 1915-04-16, and this claim records 1915-04-15, the day through whose end the order ran, consistent with the owner's inclusive reading of stated dates. Searches made on 2026-10-28: census register titles and the WPA 1944 numbered list for 1915 Lincoln or half-mast orders, and a citation search of every held order text for 'No. 2171' and 'Order No. 2171'. The only citation hit, in jobs/fr-originals/output/texts/EO_7870.txt, amends an 'Administrative Order No. 2171', a different instrument. Nothing names EO 2171. The machine USC and eCFR searches (complete, 0 hits) exclude a current-law reference; the OFR catalog search starts in 1937 and is not relied on alone.

Its command lasts as long as the named committee exists and the inspection regulations stand; neither end is shown by any held source. A held government printed copy of the Treasury decision (jobs/hathi-gpo-orders/output/texts/EO_6343.txt, filed under number 6343, T.D. 4397) restates the same 13(a) amendment and is not a later event. The WPA list shows a separate order of May 21, 1934 (EO 6712) opening returns to a House Judiciary Committee investigating receiverships; it does not name this order or the Senate committee. Clauses are quoted from that registered file, not from the clause-drafts copy. EO 6773 (June 30, 1934), read in full, exempts Carleton W. Sturtevant, principal engineer, Engineer Department at Large, War Department, from section 204 of the Act of June 30, 1932 and continues the employee in the service until November 1, 1935. The order recites that Sturtevant 'was 70 years of age on January 24, 1934' and 'was exempted from compulsory retirement for a period of 6 months by Executive Order No. 6577, dated January 25, 1934'. The machine own-terms leads dated 1934-01-24 read his seventieth birthday as a term; they are rejected, and the end cites the lead on the operative sentence ('until November 1, 1935'). Identity: number, date, person and title agree across the APP page record, the census register and the WPA 1944 numbered list. Later orders naming the same employee are held and added to this packet as source-supplement excerpts: EO 7217 (October 30, 1935) recites Executive Orders No. 6577 and No. 6773 ('a period of twenty-one months') and further exempts him until May 1, 1936; this text is a live-harvested APP page (DOCUMENTS.jsonl only, no archived capture), so its custody cannot be re-proven once the site changes. Each is recorded as a later event on the clause (clauses.csv). Extension reading, decided on the texts: each later order is a new exercise of the section 204 proviso with its own period. None says that this order 'is amended' or alters its date; each recites the earlier exemption as a past grant ('who was exempted ... by Executive Order No. ...') and grants a further exemption 'until' a new date. The strike-and-insert ruling does not apply because nothing is struck or inserted. So this order's own command ended on its own stated date, inclusive (exclusive alternative: ended when that day began), and each later order is recorded as a later event naming the same employee; the employee's exempt status continued without a gap under the later orders.
